comments.text:
Lot of people in the comments don't understand anything. 

2.  If employer matches that's 100% return. Then stocks returned 20% year over year for like 5 years. Soo you're talking 200% return in like 5 years. That means you put in $10k and it turned into $30k. 

So let's say you get a chronic illness and lose your job. You withdraw it all. They automatically take out 10% for taxes when you withdraw. Now you will owe a penalty. 

However, if 100% of that goes to pay medical bills and you can't work so you only made unemployment... The first $32,000 is tax free if you're married. So theoretically you may owe zero taxes and get a refund. 

However if you dont get the hardship withdrawal and say you got a lot of unemployment then maybe only say $10,000 of that is taxable. 

Point being, 200% return even with say 25% penalty is still 175% return. 

Locking in 175% return to pay debt at 30+% interest is a smart move. 

People don't understand numbers.
